title: Yogurt
description: Food produced by bacterial fermentation of milk
wiki_lead:
Yogurt (UK: ; US: ; Turkish: yoğurt, pronounced [joˈuɾt]), also spelled yoghurt, is a food produced by bacterial fermentation of milk. The bacteria ferment the sugars in the milk and produce lactic acid, which acts on milk protein to give yogurt its texture and characteristic tart flavor. Yogurt is most commonly made from cow's milk, but milk from water buffalo, goats, ewes, mares, camels, and yaks can also be used. 
The main bacteria used to produce yogurt are Lactobacillus delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus. Other lactobacilli and bifidobacteria are sometimes added during or after culturing yogurt. Some countries require yogurt to contain a specific amount of colony-forming units (CFU) of bacteria; for example, in China, the requirement for the number of lactobacillus bacteria is at least 1 million CFU per milliliter. Some countries also regulate which bacteria can be used: for example, in France, a product can only be labeled as yaourt or yoghourt if it has been fermented exclusively by Lactobacillus delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus, a requirement that aligns with the international definition of yogurt in the Codex Alimentarius on fermented milk (CXS 243-2003).
The bacterial culture is mixed in, and a warm temperature of 30–45 °C (86–113 °F) is maintained for 4 to 12 hours to allow fermentation to occur, with the higher temperatures working faster but risking a lumpy texture or whey separation.
wiki_fulltext:
Yogurt (UK: ; US: ; Turkish: yoğurt, pronounced [joˈuɾt]), also spelled yoghurt, is a food produced by bacterial fermentation of milk. The bacteria ferment the sugars in the milk and produce lactic acid, which acts on milk protein to give yogurt its texture and characteristic tart flavor. Yogurt is most commonly made from cow's milk, but milk from water buffalo, goats, ewes, mares, camels, and yaks can also be used. 
The main bacteria used to produce yogurt are Lactobacillus delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus. Other lactobacilli and bifidobacteria are sometimes added during or after culturing yogurt. Some countries require yogurt to contain a specific amount of colony-forming units (CFU) of bacteria; for example, in China, the requirement for the number of lactobacillus bacteria is at least 1 million CFU per milliliter. Some countries also regulate which bacteria can be used: for example, in France, a product can only be labeled as yaourt or yoghourt if it has been fermented exclusively by Lactobacillus delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus, a requirement that aligns with the international definition of yogurt in the Codex Alimentarius on fermented milk (CXS 243-2003).
The bacterial culture is mixed in, and a warm temperature of 30–45 °C (86–113 °F) is maintained for 4 to 12 hours to allow fermentation to occur, with the higher temperatures working faster but risking a lumpy texture or whey separation.


Etymology
The word, yogurt (also yoghurt with variations), is derived from Ottoman Turkish for yugurt or yoğurt, having its root yog meaning "to condense" as related to yogur (to "knead"). It was first used in English in 1625.


History


Origin
The tradition of fermenting dairy beverages that ultimately gave rise to modern yogurt goes back to millennia, beginning in the domestication of milk-producing animals in Central Asia and the Near East. Humans likely began incorporating dairy into their diets between 10,000 and 5,000 BC. Milk lipids discovered on vessel fragments at the Barcın Höyük site in northwest Turkey provide some of the oldest archaeological evidence of dairying from the Neolithic period, which have shown that early farmers were already processing, consuming, and transporting dairy products by 6600 BCE. This included the use of specialized four-legged vessels, which allowed the physical agitation necessary for churning milk to create thickened products.

Due to the rapid spoilage of milk, several methods have been developed to improve the durability of milk. The most widely accepted view in literature is that yogurt emerged through a natural fermentation caused by environmental conditions when nomadic communities carried milk in animal skin bags. Nomads are noted to have refined the fermentation process by reusing vessels and relying on indigenous microflora.
The earliest description of the use of animal skin bags to ferment milk appears in the 11th-century Karakhanid work Dīwān Lughāt al-Turk, defining kumis as "mares' milk which is poured in skins, fermented and drunk", and several containers made from animal skin (e.g. butiq, qasuq, qurluq) that were used to store kumis. A detailed description of this practice is attested by the 13th-century Franciscan friar William of Rubruck, remarking that the Mongols churned a mare's milk product called cosmos, the Latin phonetic transliteration of kumis, in a large animal skin bag with a stick until the liquid fermented and produced an alcoholic drink. In Central Asia, a traditional fermentation process of kumis involves using a horsehide (saba) or stirring the milk in a deep wooden vessel (kubi). Similarly, the German naturalist and explorer Peter Simon Pallas remarked in his 17th-century travelogue Travels Through Various Provinces of the Russian Empire that the Bashkirs constantly stored a sour milk called arjan in a large bottle-shaped animal skin. Kefir grains, historically called gypy ayran, were discovered by local residents in the North Caucasus, when milk sugars interacted with the microflora residing within the folds of the wineskin (gybyt) during transportation, although they may have been produced earlier by Bronze Age populations by around 1500 BC, when the microbial remnants of kefir grains were found in tombs of the Xiaohe Cemetery in Xinjiang, China.


Early documentation of the term yogurt
The Karakhanid works Dīwān Lughāt al-Turk and Kutadgu Bilig provide the first attestation of yogurt as an established dairy product. In Dīwān Lughāt al-Turk, Mahmud Kashgari records several expressions in relation to yoġrut, including ol yoġrut uḏitti ("he curdled the yogurt"), yoġrut qōrlandi or qoyuldi ("the curdled milk thickened"), and yoġrut sütgärdi ("the yogurt was shaken up until it became as watery as milk"). Central to this practice was qōr, a starter culture consisting of leftover yoġrut or fermented kumis retained at the bottom of a container and used to solidify fresh milk or to ferment kumis. Other recorded milk products include süzmä, qurut (or suġut), ayrān, qatiq, qanaq (or qayaq), suviq yoġrut (diluted yogurt), bulduni (thick mixture of sour and fresh milk), igdük (food made from milk and curdled milk), and iprük (mixture of curdled and fresh milk, consumed as a laxative). The Kutadgu Bilig lists yoġrut as one of the milk products provided by animal-raising people for the household.
The 14th-century Mamluk-era Egyptian cookbook Kanz al-Fawāʾid Fī Tanwīʿ Al-Mawāʾid (Arabic: كنز الفوائد في تنويع الموائد) reveals a recipe for yoġrut under the Arabic name laban yāghurt (Arabic: لبن ياغرت). The preparation involved boiling cow’s or water buffalo’s milk, allowing it to cool, and then adding a starter culture consisting of very sour milk and water-dissolved rennet. The mixture was transferred into vessels to ferment, taking approximately 12 hours to set (either from morning to evening, or overnight).


Fermented milk and early yogurt-like products in antiquity
Ancient Greek and Roman authors from the Classical period associated dairying with peoples whom they regarded as "barbarians". Notably, Pliny the Elder remarked that "barbarian nations" knew how "to thicken the milk into a substance with an agreeable acidity". Greeks and Romans disliked milk products and regarded them as unimportant, due to a combination of cultural taboos, viewing milk-drinking as a barbaric trait, and environmental factors, such as the rapid spoilage of milk in warm Mediterranean climates, and a biological intolerance to lactose. Similarly, William of Rubruck recorded that the devoted Orthodox Christians living near or under the Mongol frontiers, including the Alans, Georgians, Greeks, Russians, and Ruthenians, restrained from drinking kumis, regarding it as an act of infidelity to the Christian faith.
In Classical literature, the Scythians were notable for their consumption and fermentation of milk, whom the Greeks became acquainted with through Black Sea colonies from the 7th century BC onward. Authors who documented them include Hesiod, Homer, Herodotus, Hippocrates, and Aeschylus. In the Iliad, Homeric expressions, such as Hippemolgi (mare-milkers) and Galactophagi (curd-eaters), were later identified with the Scythians by the ancient Greek geographer Strabo. The Botai culture of northern Kazakhstan provides some of the first archaeological evidence of mare's milk consumption and practicing by around 3500 BC, when fats of mare's milk were found on pottery.
Drinking fermented mare's milk was the daily norm for the Scythians, while the Greeks consumed it for medicinal purposes. Greek authors displayed familiarity with the Scythian milk-processing and its nutritional and therapeutic peculiarities, incorporating them into Greek medical literature by the 5th century BC. For example, the Hippocratic text De affectionibus interioribus prescribes the daily consumption of "agitated horse milk" to treat tuberculosis, whose process resembled the initial stages of the Scythian cheese-like or sour horse milk product called hippake. Herodotus' description of Scythian fermented mare's milk is believed to have described kumis. Greek knowledge of the Scythian dietary likely developed through the experiences of Greek settlers and traders in the Black Sea.
Oxygala (Greek: ὀξύγαλα, lit. 'sour milk') was a fermented milk product well-known in the Hellenistic and Roman periods. Its precise nature remains uncertain, as Ancient Greek, Latin, and Byzantine texts utilized the term oxygala variously for products that have undergone a process of fermentation. Modern scholars have identified oxygala as a product resembling yogurt, cheese or curd, and xinogala (Greek: ξινόγαλα), a modern Greek beverage regarded as synonymous of ayran. The product was considered suitable for consumption in the Greek and Roman diet because it was thought to be easier to digest. However, to counteract its  potential harmful effects, such as dentin hypersensitivity and kidney stones, the 2nd-century physician Galen recommended mixing it with honey. One of the earliest references to oxygala appears in a surviving fragment from the Philippica by the 4th-century BC Greek historian Theopompus, preserved by Hesychius of Alexandria. The passage describes oxygala hippeion (Greek: ὀξύγαλα ἵππειον, lit. 'sour mare's milk') as a food consumed by the Scythians, both as a drink and iin solidified form. A more detailed description of oxygala is found in the 1st-century De re rustica by the Roman author Columella, which appears to have produced quark or cottage cheese. Pliny the Elder describes oxygala as a solid curd by-product that was obtained when butter was made. Later Greek authors, such as Oribasius, Aëtius of Amida, Anthimus, and Paul of Aegina, and the Byzantine agricultural treatise Geoponica, mention oxygala as a medical remedy.
The Rigveda (Sanskrit: ऋग्वेद), an ancient Indian collection from the Vedic period, contains early references to dahi (Sanskrit: दधि)., which is considered to be the equivalent of modern curd or yogurt. The text outlines two ways of producing dahi, either by using the backslopping method, which uses a portion of a previous batch as a starter culture, or by adding vegetal material, such as putika, kuvala, or the bark of palasha. The Rigveda credits dahi with providing good nutrition, helping digestion, and treating gastrointestinal issues, such as diarrhea and dysentery.
One of the earliest historical references to processed dairy in China appears in the 1st century BC Chinese collection Book of Rites, where a preserved milk product called lǐlào (Chinese: 醴酪) is recognized as a skill integrated into early Chinese civilization. During the Han dynasty, Chinese sources record the preparation of a fermented yogurt called lào (Chinese: 酪), made from cow and sheep milk, noting that the product and the word lào was adopted from Central Asian pastoralists that lived along the northern and northwestern frontiers of modern-day China. Around the same period, the Book of Han describes the Hu ren (Chinese: 胡人) as a nomadic people, without a land or city to their name, who "eat meat and drink yogurt". The 6th-century book Qimin Yaoshu, compiled during the Northern Wei dynasty, contains detailed instructions for making lào, which involves boiling slowly and continuously stirring the raw milk, straining the cooked milk into clay bottles, inoculating the milk with a sweet yogurt starter or a sour porridge paste as a substituting once cooled, and wrapping the vessels in felt or wadding to insulate them overnight until the yogurt sets. It also gives methods for producing variations, including gānlào (Chinese: 乾酪, lit. 'dried curdled milk') and lùlào (Chinese: 漉酪, lit. 'strained curdled milk'), and for the starter, mǎlào jiào (Chinese: 馬酪酵, lit. 'mares' milk starter').
Julius Caesar, in his 1st-century book Commentarii de Bello Gallico, observed that the Germanic diet consisted mainly of products from their flocks and herds
grok_lead: Yogurt is a fermented dairy product produced by culturing one or more basic dairy ingredientsâsuch as cream, milk, partially skimmed milk, or skim milk âwith the bacterial cultures Lactobacillus delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus. These cultures convert lactose in the milk into lactic acid, resulting in a semisolid consistency with a pH of 4.6 or lower, which contributes to its tangy flavor and extended shelf life. The product must contain at least 8.25% milk solids not fat and typically 3.25% milkfat, though variations exist based on regulatory standards and processing. Originating around 6000 BCE among nomadic herdsmen in Western Asia and the Middle East, yogurt likely developed when milk stored in animal-skin pouches naturally fermented due to ambient bacteria. The term "yogurt" derives from the Turkish word yoÄurmak, meaning "to thicken," reflecting its cultural significance in regions like Turkey, Iran, and Mesopotamia. By the early 20th century, Bulgarian scientist Stamen Grigorov isolated Lactobacillus bulgaricus (now classified as L. delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus), advancing scientific understanding and commercial production of the food. Today, yogurt is a global staple, consumed in various forms and integral to diets in Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, Central Asian, and Indian subcontinental cuisines. The production process begins with heating milk to 110â115Â°F (43â46Â°C) to pasteurize it and denature proteins, followed by cooling and inoculation with starter cultures that ferment the mixture for at least four hours until the desired acidity is achieved. Optional ingredients like sweeteners, flavorings, or stabilizers may be added, and the yogurt can be homogenized or strained for texture variations. Common types include plain yogurt, Greek yogurt (strained to remove whey, yielding higher protein content), low-fat or nonfat versions, and plant-based alternatives made from soy, almond, or coconut milk, though the latter may not always meet traditional dairy standards. Greek yogurt, for instance, contains about twice the protein of regular yogurt due to the straining process. Nutritionally, yogurt is a nutrient-dense food providing high-quality protein (8â10 grams per 8-ounce serving), calcium, phosphorus, potassium, vitamin B12, and riboflavin, with fermentation reducing lactose content to make it more digestible for lactose-intolerant individuals. It also serves as a source of probiotics âlive beneficial bacteriaâthat support gut microbiota diversity and may alleviate digestive issues like irritable bowel syndrome. Regular consumption has been associated with reduced risks of type 2 diabetes (up to 18% lower) and obesity in large cohort studies, attributed to its effects on blood sugar regulation and satiety. Observational studies and meta-analyses also associate regular yogurt consumption with reduced all-cause and cardiovascular mortality risk, such as a 7% lower all-cause mortality for high versus low intake. However, flavored varieties often contain added sugars, including some Greek yogurts with cereals that have excess added sugars; these are not suitable for individuals managing high cholesterol, as added sugars can contribute to elevated triglycerides and increased cardiovascular risks. Plain low-fat or nonfat options, particularly Greek yogurt without added sugars, are recommended for optimal health benefits and cholesterol management. These can be paired with various complementary foods to enhance nutritional benefits through synergistic effects. For example, combining yogurt with fresh fruits such as bananas, berries, and kiwi provides prebiotics like fructo-oligosaccharides and polyphenols that enhance the survival, activity, and colonization of yogurt's probiotics in the gut, leading to improved gut health and nutrient absorption. Pairing with oats or barley adds soluble fiber such as beta-glucan, which supports intestinal health by promoting beneficial gut bacteria. Nuts and seeds contribute healthy fats and additional protein, while honey provides prebiotic compounds and protects probiotic bacteria during digestion. Specific pairings include yogurt with blueberries, supplying antioxidants that support eye health, and with pumpkin, combining yogurt's calcium with pumpkin's beta-carotene and other nutrients to support blood pressure regulation. Additionally, consumption of plain low-fat yogurt has been associated with lower serum triglyceride levels, likely due to probiotics, calcium, and other nutrients, and is beneficial for managing high uric acid levels, as it is low in purines and milk proteins promote uric acid excretion, potentially reducing gout risk.
